Composite materials are defined as materials consisting of two or more distinct constituent materials.
Graphite/epoxy, boron/epoxy, aramid/epoxy, and glass/epoxy are the main composite materials used in aircraft structures.
Graphite/epoxy and aramid/epoxy are the most important for structural applications.
Composite materials offer weight savings of up to 25% compared to conventional metals.
The main joining methods for composite structures are mechanical fastening and adhesive bonding.
Hybrid repair methods combine adhesives and fasteners to enhance structural performance.
Typical repair methods include scarf repair, step repair, patch repair, and resin injection.
Scarf repair is used for major structural repairs and results in a flush repair.
Resin injection is often used for delamination and is considered a temporary measure.
External repairs (doubler) are applied to the outside of the structure and are suited for thin components or skins.
Internal repairs (flush) are applied inside and are used for thick laminates.
Damage tolerance is crucial for composite materials due to their susceptibility to low-energy impacts.
Common NDI methods include ultrasonic testing, radiography, and visual inspection.
Composite materials are used in the skins of horizontal and vertical tails, wing skins, control surfaces, and fuselage components in military aircraft.
Composite materials are used in control surfaces, fairings, and some primary structures in civil aircraft.
The matrix in composite materials serves to bond the fibers and transfer loads between them.
Environmental effects, fatigue, and damage tolerance are key factors affecting the in-service performance of composite aircraft structures.
The scarf method involves tapering the laminates as the damaged area is removed, resulting in a flush repair.
Airworthiness certification of aircraft with composite components requires consideration of structural integrity, repair effectiveness, and inspection and maintenance capabilities.
Specialized training and expertise are required for repairing composite structures.
The difficulty in preparing repair patches for complex shapes is a challenge in composite repair.
Proper bonding and curing are essential to maintain the structural integrity of composite repairs.
Composite materials can be used in both secondary and primary structures in aircraft.
The use of composite materials in aircraft structures is expected to increase in the future.
